notes.meaning: In the ancient world, an animal's horn stood for strength, and an arm stood for the power to swing a sword. The Lord declares that Moab's power has been stripped away and its military strength completely broken. The nation can no longer defend its borders or strike at its enemies.

The Lord tells the invaders to pour out judgment like a cup of strong drink until Moab collapses in helpless confusion. Because the nation proudly exalted itself against God, it will sink into shame and disgust. Moab will become a laughingstock to the surrounding world, suffering the same scorn it once poured on others.

God asks Moab why it treated Israel with such mockery and contempt during its downfall. Israel had not been caught stealing like a common thief, so Moab had no right to shake its head with cruel joy over its neighbor's disaster. Gloating over the suffering of God's people brings His righteous discipline.

The people of Moab are told to leave their cities and run to high, rocky cliffs for shelter. Like wild doves that build their nests safe in the clefts of deep ravines, the refugees must hide in remote caverns. Their strong city walls will no longer protect them from the invading army.

The Lord describes how widely known Moab was for its extreme arrogance and proud heart. The prophet piles up different words for pride to show how deeply this sin had taken root in the nation. Despite earlier warnings, the people refused to humble themselves before God.
God knows all about Moab's angry threats and arrogant schemes, but none of them will succeed. Their proud boasts are completely empty, and their deceitful words cannot protect them from coming ruin.

Even though Moab richly deserves its punishment, the prophet weeps with deep sorrow over the terrible scene. A loud wailing goes out for the whole country, especially for the fortress city of Kir-heres. God's messengers do not take delight in ruin, but feel the heavy weight of human suffering.

Sibmah was celebrated across the region for its lush vineyards that stretched across valleys toward nearby towns. The prophet mourns because an invader will suddenly sweep in and strip the vines bare. The rich harvest of summer fruit and grapes will be wiped out in an instant.

All gladness and singing vanish from the fruitful fields and orchards of Moab. The Lord puts a complete stop to the winepresses, so no workers will stomp the grapes with merry songs. The joyful shouts of harvest are replaced by the terrifying cries of attacking soldiers.

Cries of panic echo from one town to the next, spreading from the north all the way to the southern borders. The weeping sounds like the desperate cries of a young cow wandering in search of her lost calf. Even the local streams and water springs dry up, leaving the refugees without relief.

The Lord declares that He will put an end to the false worship that covered the land. The priests and people who climbed up to hill shrines to burn sacrifices to idols will be removed. Their pagan gods will prove entirely helpless to save them from judgment.

The prophet's heart groans with a low, mournful sound like funeral flutes playing sad music. He laments over the people of Kir-heres because all the wealth and savings they worked hard to gather have vanished overnight. Material riches cannot provide lasting security when God's judgment arrives.

The people of Moab show the deepest outward signs of grief common in the ancient East. They shave their heads and trim their beards, cut their hands in anguish, and wrap rough sackcloth around their waists. These acts reveal a nation overwhelmed by total loss.

Crowds gather on their flat rooftops and in the town squares to weep aloud in public view. The Lord explains that He has shattered Moab just like an unwanted clay jar that a potter throws away as useless. The nation has lost its honor and usefulness because of its stubborn rebellion.

Onlookers cry out in shock at how thoroughly Moab has been broken and turned away in disgrace. The nation that once laughed at the trouble of others has now become a mockery to some and a terrifying lesson to everyone else.

The Lord compares King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon to a great eagle diving swiftly toward its prey. The conqueror will spread his vast wings over the entire land of Moab, leaving the people no time to react or defend themselves.

Fortified cities and high mountain strongholds are quickly captured by the invading army. Moab's seasoned fighters lose all their courage, overcome by sudden terror like a woman gripped by labor pains.
Moab will cease to exist as an independent, organized nation. This collapse comes because the people proudly exalted themselves against the Lord rather than honoring Him.
The Lord warns the residents of Moab that inescapable traps surround them on every side. Hunted like animals in the wild, they will run from sudden terror only to face pits and concealed snares.

Anyone who flees the initial panic will fall into a pit, and anyone who climbs out will get caught in a hidden trap. God has appointed a specific time of reckoning for Moab, making it impossible to evade His righteous judgment.

Exhausted refugees run toward the fortified city of Heshbon hoping to find protection under its shadow, but they find only disappointment. A consuming fire of war breaks out from Heshbon, devouring the leaders and noisy crowds of Moab just as ancient war songs once described.
A cry of sorrow rings out because the people who trusted in their idol Chemosh are ruined. Their false god is powerless to help them, and their sons and daughters are marched away into captivity.
Even after severe judgment, the Lord makes a promise of future mercy. He declares that in days to come He will bring Moab back from exile and restore its fortunes.

differ.view: Methodists traditionally understand this restoration in a spiritual sense, pointing to the Gentiles being called into the kingdom of the Messiah.
Some evangelicals expect a literal future restoration of Moabite descendants to their former land during the thousand-year earthly reign of Christ.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Modern scholars generally regard the closing sentence as an editorial note added to mark the end of the prophecies against Moab.
